content: 1. Pregnant women, mothers, families, and healthcare workers must be safeguarded from exploitative marketing practices by manufacturers and distributors of breast-milk substitutes. 2. Healthcare providers should possess the necessary knowledge and skills to support breastfeeding mothers with evidence-based care. 3. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) determined that there is insufficient evidence to make recommendations regarding the use of full-fat versus low-fat milk or animal milk versus plant-based milk for children aged 12–23 months. 4. Sweetened milks, which contain added sugars, are not suitable for infants and young children aged 6–23 months. 5. For infants aged 6–11 months who are not breastfed, either milk formula or animal milk can be used, though this recommendation is conditional and based on low-certainty evidence. 6. For children aged 12–23 months who are not breastfed, animal milk is recommended, while follow-up formulas are not advised. This recommendation is also conditional and based on low-certainty evidence. 7. Dairy products, including liquid animal milk, are important components of a diverse diet and contribute to nutritional adequacy, especially for non-breastfed children in settings where other animal-source foods are unavailable. 8. Acceptable types of animal milk include pasteurized animal milk, reconstituted evaporated milk (but not condensed milk), fermented milk, or yogurt. 9. Flavored or sweetened milks should not be used. 10. If infants aged 6–11 months are fed animal milk, full-fat milk should be used. 11. Safe storage and handling practices for animal milk must be followed. 12. Complementary foods should be introduced to infants at 6 months of age (180 days) while continuing breastfeeding. This is a strong recommendation, though based on low-certainty evidence. 13. Some infants may benefit from earlier introduction of complementary foods, but this should be assessed on an individual basis. 14. Mothers concerned about the adequacy of their breast milk supply may benefit from lactation support. 15. While iron in breast milk is highly bioavailable, some infants, particularly those born preterm or with low birth weight, may be at risk of iron deficiency. Early introduction of complementary foods, even if iron-fortified, does not adequately prevent iron deficiency anemia in high-risk populations. 16. Infants and young children aged 6–23 months should consume a diverse diet. 17. Animal-source foods, such as meat, fish, or eggs, should be consumed daily. 18. Fruits and vegetables should also be consumed daily. 19. Pulses, nuts, and seeds should be consumed frequently, especially when animal-source foods and vegetables are limited in the diet. 20. Animal-source foods, fruits, vegetables, nuts, pulses, and seeds should be prioritized in the diet due to their higher nutrient density compared to cereal grains. 21. Starchy staple foods should be minimized, as they often lack high-quality proteins and critical nutrients like iron, zinc, and vitamin B12. Many also contain anti-nutrients that reduce nutrient absorption. 22. When cereal grains are used, whole grains should be prioritized, and refined grains minimized. 23. Pulses, nuts, and seeds should be prepared in forms that do not pose a choking risk. 24. Foods high in sugar, salt, and trans fats should not be consumed. 25. Sugar-sweetened beverages should not be consumed. 26. Non-sugar sweeteners should not be consumed. 27. Consumption of 100% fruit juice should be limited. 28. Nutrient supplements or fortified food products may be beneficial for children aged 6–23 months in contexts where nutrient requirements cannot be met through unfortified foods alone. 29. Multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) can provide additional vitamins and minerals without displacing other foods in the diet. 30. Fortification of commercial cereal-based complementary foods and blended flours can improve micronutrient intake but should not be encouraged as a primary dietary source. 31. Small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) may be useful in food-insecure populations with significant nutritional deficiencies. 32. None of these products should be distributed as stand-alone interventions; they must be accompanied by messaging and complementary support to reinforce optimal infant and young child feeding practices. 33. These products are not substitutes for a diverse diet consisting of healthy and minimally processed foods. 34. Responsive feeding practices should be encouraged for children aged 6–23 months. This involves feeding that supports the child’s autonomy and responds to their physiological and developmental needs, promoting self-regulation in eating and supporting cognitive, emotional, and social development. 35. Healthcare workers and caregivers must be equipped to provide guidance on responsive feeding practices. 36. Caregivers should have the time and resources to be present during feeding and to manage food loss during self-feeding. 37. There is limited evidence for many of the recommendations, highlighting the need for more research using standardized protocols across diverse populations and contexts. 38. Complementary feeding, defined as the process of introducing foods when breast milk or formula alone is no longer sufficient to meet nutritional needs, typically begins at 6 months and continues until 23 months of age. 39. This period is critical for children to learn to accept healthy foods and beverages and establish long-term dietary patterns. 40. It is also a peak period for the risk of growth faltering and nutrient deficiencies, with immediate consequences such as impaired growth, morbidity, mortality, and delayed motor, cognitive, and socio-emotional development. 41. Early childhood undernutrition can lead to long-term consequences, including reduced work capacity, earnings, and reproductive capacity, as well as increased risk of noncommunicable diseases. 42. Inappropriate complementary feeding can result in overweight, type 2 diabetes, and disability in adulthood. 43. The first two years of life are critical for brain development, language acquisition, and the development of sensory pathways and higher cognitive functions. 44. Appropriate complementary feeding is essential for achieving global nutrition targets, including reducing stunting, wasting, and childhood overweight. 45. This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for complementary feeding of infants and young children aged 6–23 months, applicable globally across low-, middle-, and high-income countries. 46. The guideline is intended for policymakers, healthcare professionals, caregivers, and organizations involved in infant and young child feeding programs. 47. It emphasizes the importance of addressing the needs of both breastfed and non-breastfed children while recognizing the necessity of individualized management to address undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, overweight, or obesity. 48. The guideline does not address the needs of preterm or low-birth-weight infants, children recovering from acute malnutrition or serious illness, or those living in emergencies, as these are covered in other WHO guidelines. 49. The guideline is food-based and does not specify nutrient levels or quantities of foods to be consumed, as these vary by age, activity level, metabolism, and local contexts. 50. It updates previous WHO guidelines to address both undernutrition and the increasing prevalence of overweight and obesity in children globally.
